data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a methodological rule for error elimination, not an inductive inference about truth probability.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the scientist acts on the theory expecting it to succeed in future applications based solely on past success, they have slipped into induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'preference' implies assigning a higher subjective degree of belief (Bayesian posterior) to the corroborated theory, it contradicts Popper's anti-probabilism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the choice is made because the theory is 'safer' or 'more reliable' in a pragmatic sense derived from past frequency, this is inductive.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Corroboration reports the severity of tests survived. Preferring the theory that has withstood more severe tests is equivalent to preferring the theory that has been less likely to be false if it were false. This is a deductive assessment of past performance (the test history), not a probabilistic prediction of future success. The 'preference' is a decision to subject the bold conjecture to further risk, maximizing the chance of finding error, rather than assuming it will hold.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
